podcast.body: Released in November 1978 under the name The Normal, this song was recorded by Daniel Miller in his bedroom using a Korg 700S synthesizer and a 4-track reel-to-reel machine, despite his lack of traditional musical experience. It became a hit, selling 30,000 copies after Rough Trade record shop in Notting Hill agreed to stock a test pressing, intriguing many young musicians with its minimalist, futuristic, and attitude-filled sound. "After it came out in November 1978, the record became a hit."

podcast.body: Released in November 1978, this track was created by Daniel Miller, who combined elements from Kraftwerk, Lou Reed, and Giorgio Moroder. It contributed to the developing "cold, distant" sound that captured a dystopian view of the future amidst a brutal recession and the Cold War. "It's also worth a reminder of the Normals' warm leatherette from November 1978."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This seven-inch single, released by Daniel Miller's one-man synth band project The Normal, sold 30,000 copies. The profits from this single were reinvested into Mute Records, which Miller had founded to release his own music. "He had a one-man synth band project called The Normal. And the only way he could interest anyone in what he was doing was to do it all himself. So he created mute, struck a deal with rough trade record shops, and ended up selling 30,000 copies of a seven-inch single called Warm Leatherette."

podcast.body: This single was composed and recorded by Daniel Miller in his bedroom and became a substantial UK hit, demonstrating the viability of independent, electronically produced music. "Daniel Miller, the solitary member of a band known as The Normal from 1978 with Warm Leatherette, a single that became a substantial UK hit that year, and a song that was composed and recorded in Daniel's bedroom."

podcast.body: This single was made by Daniel Miller in his bedroom using inexpensive keyboards. He initially pressed 500 copies and sold them on consignment, which eventually grew to 25,000 copies and generated enough money for him to found Mute Records. "The guy is Daniel Miller. He made that single in his bedroom with some cheap keyboards. He pressed up some singles, sold them on consignment through a bunch of record stores, 500 copies became a thousand and then 5,000 and I've heard his highest 25,000."
